title: Storyboard Template PDF: Blank and Filled-In Boards
summary: A storyboard template PDF layout, plus real filled-in boards from Flick films: 10-frame grids, a scene sheet and hand-drawn panels, each with its frames.
body_markdown:
### What is a storyboard template?


A storyboard template is a blank page of frames, each in the film's aspect ratio, with numbered boxes and lines under each for the shot size, action and dialogue. You fill it in to plan a scene shot by shot before filming or generating anything.


### How many frames should a storyboard template have?


Six frames to a page is the usual layout, because it leaves room to write under each frame. A short scene often fits ten frames on one sheet, which is how the maker of the Flick residency film Battery Boy laid out each of his boards.


### What should I write under each storyboard frame?


Write the shot size and camera angle, one line of action in the present tense and any dialogue or sound in quotes. Add the emotion the shot should carry when it matters, and keep notes that apply to every shot in one strip at the bottom of the page.


### What aspect ratio should storyboard frames be?


Draw the frames in the shape of the finished film, usually 16:9 for online video and television, or 2.39:1 for a widescreen film. A frame in the wrong shape hides how much space surrounds a character, which is what the board is meant to show.


### Do I need to draw well to make a storyboard?


No drawing skill is needed: boxes and stick figures work if they show where the camera sits and how big each figure is. Photos, a 3D blockout or an AI image of each shot can also fill the frames.


### What is the difference between a storyboard and a shot list?


A shot list is a written table with one row per shot: its size, angle, movement and action. A storyboard draws each of those shots as a frame, so it shows what a shot list cannot, such as how big a figure is and what stands in front of what.


### Can I make a storyboard with AI?


Yes. An image model can draw each frame from a one-line description and a character reference, and in Flick each frame sits on a canvas in story order, where it can become the start of the shot it plans.
